title: 2025 budget: housing, climate growth and deferred expansions
subtitle: Grand River Conservation Authority draft budget, housing debt costs, transit and water rates, and a call for provincial funding
overview: The Strategic Planning and Budget Committee reviewed the Homes for All and Climate Aligned Growth parts of the 2025 plan and budget. Staff said the base budget increase is $58.1 million, a 9.3 percent tax impact. Proposed expansions would bring the combined impact to about 12 percent. These figures are preliminary and no final decisions were made. Final budget day is December 11.

The committee recommended moving a group of transportation, waste, energy and sustainability expansions to the November 27 budget deliberations {{vote:m2}}. It deferred five housing and infrastructure expansions to November 27 {{vote:m1}}, and deferred the user-rate-supported water and wastewater positions to the same date {{vote:m3}}. Members said they wanted to see all staffing requests together before choosing.

Committee members heard that completing the Waterloo Region Housing revitalization plan could bring about $37.4 million a year in debt servicing by 2031. Members also asked Council, through the Regional Chair's office, to press area MPPs for a funding deal like those given to Toronto and Ottawa {{vote:m6}}. The committee also received the Grand River Conservation Authority's draft budget for information.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended deferring five tax-supported expansions to November 27: affordable housing resources, WRH insurability staff, the plan to end chronic homelessness, employment pilot transition funding and a senior engineer.

The committee recommended moving a package of tax-supported expansions to November 27 budget deliberations, including transit network improvements, MobilityPLUS capacity, GRT support staff, automated cart collection positions and sustainability staffing.

decisions.item: Water and wastewater staff positions deferred
decisions.detail: The committee recommended deferring the user-rate-supported water and wastewater expansions, such as specialists, hydrogeologists, students and a cyber security analyst, to November 27.

The committee recommended that the Region ask, through the Regional Chair's office, that the five area MPPs seek a fair funding deal like those for Toronto and Ottawa, and share the resolution with area municipalities.

debate: Several councillors raised concern about debt for the WRH revitalization plan, with servicing costs peaking in 2031. Staff said housing is not eligible for development charges, so the debt falls on the tax levy. Staff added that only the 2025 capital program is approved, and options include phasing, grant conditions or longer debentures.

Supporters of deferring the staffing requests said new positions should be judged together against the overall tax impact. Another councillor said jobs help the community and economy, and a third noted deferral to November 27 still allows line-by-line review.

On water and wastewater, one councillor said user rates and taxes are paid by the same household and should be reviewed together. Staff said the positions are funded from rates, not the levy, and recommended keeping rates and adding any savings to the infrastructure reserve.

Staff said rent supplements are very effective at housing people but depend on available units and landlords, and cannot replace building new housing. Staff also said the Region's shelter plan assumes King Street closes in March, with 84 Frederick opening as a women's shelter.

On the funding motion, members said municipalities carry costs the province covers elsewhere and pointed to AMO's advocacy. One councillor noted past motions to MPPs have drawn no replies, and another said Kitchener already has regular dialogue with both levels of government.
